implementation_notes: CPython exposes no compare-and-swap or atomic load/store, so a pure-Python CAS loop cannot be written: the only published atomicity is per-operation (deque.append/popleft, list.append) under the GIL, and the queue module's documentation states that its classes implement the locking semantics internally with locks. A lock-free queue therefore exists only inside C extensions, and even free-threaded builds add no public CAS. The GIL also removes the main motivation: for I/O-bound hand-off queue.SimpleQueue (unbounded, C implementation, reentrant) or Queue(maxsize=n) with blocking put/get is fast and correct, and for CPU parallelism the right structure is multiprocessing.Queue or a process pool rather than a ring shared between threads that cannot run in parallel.
alternative: queue.SimpleQueue (C-implemented, mutex-based, reentrant) or collections.deque with atomic append/popleft under the GIL; for CPU parallelism use multiprocessing.Queue or concurrent.futures instead of emulating compare-and-swap.
code_sketch:
from queue import SimpleQueue
q = SimpleQueue()          # unbounded, lock-based, C implementation, reentrant
q.put(item)                # never blocks, always succeeds (allocation aside)
item = q.get()             # blocks until an item arrives
# bounded alternative: Queue(maxsize=1024) - put() blocks, giving backpressure
pitfalls: Per-operation atomicity is not a transaction: if q.empty(): q.get() races other consumers, so use get_nowait() or timeouts instead of check-then-act.
Queue's locks are not designed for reentrancy: a callback that puts into the same queue from inside a put/get path can deadlock.
qsize()/empty()/full() are approximate and must not gate control flow, and on some platforms a blocking get() is uninterruptible.
